title: Buckley v. Valeo (1976) — appointments holding
summary: Congress could not vest significant administration and enforcement powers in Federal Election Commissioners appointed through a process inconsistent with Article II.

sections.Parties: Challengers to the Federal Election Campaign Act and related provisions disputed the authority of the Federal Election Commission. The Commission defended its statutory appointment structure and powers. The supplied excerpt addresses appointments rather than the case’s separate campaign-finance merits.
sections.Material Facts: The eight-member Commission included six voting members: two selected by the President, two by the Senate’s President pro tempore, and two by the House Speaker, with confirmation by both chambers. Two congressional officers served ex officio without votes. The Commission could collect and investigate information, prescribe rules, issue advisory opinions with protective legal effects, determine eligibility, and initiate civil litigation. These substantial powers made the method of selection constitutionally consequential.
sections.Procedural History: The case reached the Supreme Court on appeals raising constitutional challenges to the campaign-finance legislation. The court of appeals had accepted an argument for Congress’s inherent authority to appoint officials serving its institutional needs. The Supreme Court rejected that argument for the Commission’s administrative and enforcement functions.
sections.Issue: Could officials selected through congressional appointments and confirmation by both chambers exercise the Commission’s significant statutory authority?
sections.Holding: Only officers appointed through the Appointments Clause could exercise its substantial administration and enforcement powers. The existing Commission could perform investigative and informational functions of the kind Congress could assign to its own committees.
sections.Reasoning: The Court defined an officer by significant authority exercised under federal law, distinguishing subordinate employees and legislative assistance. The President’s nominees were subject to an unconstitutional extra House confirmation requirement; congressional leaders were not authorized Article II appointing actors. Congress’s power to create offices and enact necessary-and-proper legislation remained subject to the express appointment rules. Seeking judicial enforcement of public law was especially clearly executive, and rulemaking, legally consequential advice, and eligibility decisions were likewise significant governmental duties. The decision therefore classified powers as well as personnel: allowing Congress to gather information did not allow its appointees to administer the entire regulatory program.

topics.lrs-s-appointments-clause: The Clause specifies the permissible appointing actors and excludes Congress from appointments to offices exercising significant federal authority.
topics.lrs-s-officer-employee: Rulemaking, legally consequential administration, and enforcement crossed the line from legislative assistance to significant governmental authority.
